title: Pain Management Mastery: Reclaiming Your Life
summary: A compassionate, scientifically grounded CBT program for living well with chronic pain. Moving beyond the medical model, this program helps you decouple pain from suffering. You will learn to break the 'boom-bust' cycle, challenge fear-based thoughts, and retrain your nervous system to dial down the volume of pain while reclaiming a life of value.

modules.title: Module 1 • Understanding Pain: The Volume Knob
modules.overview: We begin by validating your experience: Your pain is real. However, we introduce the difference between acute pain (damage) and chronic pain (system sensitivity). The 'Gate Control Theory' of pain is explained. You will learn how your brain and spinal cord act as a gate that can open (amplifying pain) or close (reducing pain) based on emotional and cognitive factors. We explore the 'Pain Cycle'—how pain leads to inactivity, which leads to stiffness and depression, which leads to more pain. Seeing the cycle allows us to spot the exit points. The concept of 'Central Sensitization' is introduced using the volume knob metaphor. Your alarm system is stuck on 'High,' detecting danger where there is none. You will start an 'Activity & Pain Log.' Unlike a standard pain diary, this tracks what you were doing, thinking, and feeling when pain levels changed. We differentiate between 'Hurt' and 'Harm.' In chronic pain, hurting does not always mean you are damaging your body. This crucial distinction opens the door to movement. Finally, we set the goal: The aim isn't necessarily zero pain (which may not be possible), but maximum life. We shift focus from 'curing' to 'living.'
takeaways: Chronic pain acts more like a sensitive alarm system than a damage detector.
Thoughts and emotions can physically open the 'pain gate' in the spinal cord.
Hurt does not equal Harm; you can be sore and safe at the same time.
Breaking the cycle starts with understanding the mechanism.
exercises: The Baseline Log: Track your pain (0-10) alongside your activity and mood 3 times a day for a week. Look for patterns: Does stress increase pain? Does distraction lower it?
The Gate Analysis: List 3 things that seem to 'open' your pain gate (make it worse) and 3 things that 'close' it (make it better). Be specific (e.g., 'Cold weather,' 'Talking to a friend').
Hurt vs. Harm Reflection: Write down one activity you avoid because of pain. Ask yourself: 'If I did this, would I be damaged, or just sore?'
homework: Complete the Baseline Log for 7 days.
Share the concept of 'Hurt vs. Harm' with a family member so they understand your new approach to movement.
Identify one 'Gate Closer' activity and do it deliberately when pain is mild.

modules.title: Module 2 • Pacing: Breaking the Boom-Bust Cycle
modules.overview: This module addresses the most common behavioral trap in chronic pain: The Boom-Bust Cycle. Overdoing it on 'good days' and crashing on 'bad days.' We introduce 'Time-Contingent' vs. 'Pain-Contingent' activity. You will learn to stop based on a plan, not based on pain. You will calculate your 'Baselines' for common activities (sitting, standing, walking). Finding the safe amount you can do without flaring. The concept of 'The Sweet Spot' is explained—finding the middle ground between inactivity (rust) and overactivity (bust). We create a Pacing Plan. Breaking large tasks into small, manageable chunks with mandatory rest breaks. We address the guilt of resting. You will learn that rest is a strategic tool for productivity, not laziness. Finally, we practice 'Graded Activity.' Slowly increasing your baselines over time to retrain the nervous system's tolerance.
takeaways: Pushing through pain on good days leads to long recovery periods (the Bust).
Pacing means stopping *before* the pain spikes, not after.
Rest breaks should be scheduled, not just taken when you collapse.
Consistency is more important than intensity.
exercises: Find Your Baselines: Measure how long you can do an activity (e.g., washing dishes) before pain flares. Do this for 3 days. Your baseline is roughly 80% of the average.
Create a Rest Schedule: Plan a task (e.g., gardening). Schedule a 5-minute break every 15 minutes. Set a timer. Obey the timer.
The 10% Rule: Plan to increase one activity by just 10% next week. (e.g., walk 11 minutes instead of 10).
homework: Implement time-contingent pacing for one major activity (e.g., walking or computer work) all week.
Catch yourself in a 'Boom' mindset (doing too much) and deliberately stop early.
Practice 'Active Rest'—during breaks, breathe or stretch, don't just scroll on your phone.

modules.title: Module 3 • The Mind-Body Connection: Turning Down the Volume
modules.overview: This module focuses on the physiological arousal that accompanies pain. Pain causes stress, and stress causes muscle tension, which causes more pain. We introduce Diaphragmatic Breathing to activate the parasympathetic nervous system and lower the body's alarm state. Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR) is adapted for pain. Learning to release the 'guarding' tension we hold around painful areas. We explore 'Visualisation' and 'Imagery.' Using the mind to create soothing sensations (warmth, coolness, flow) in painful areas. The concept of 'Solicitous Responses' is discussed. How the reactions of others (over-helping or ignoring) affect our pain experience. We address sleep, which is often disrupted by pain. Basic sleep hygiene strategies are applied to the pain context. Finally, we practice 'Mindfulness of Sensation.' observing the raw sensation of pain without the emotional label of 'suffering.'
takeaways: A relaxed body perceives less pain than a tense body.
Guarding (tensing up) around a painful area restricts blood flow and increases stiffness.
Visualization can hack the brain's sensory processing areas.
Mindfulness changes the relationship to pain from victim to observer.
exercises: Body Scan for Tension: Scan your body. Are you holding your jaw tight? Are your shoulders up? Drop them. Do this 5 times a day.
Softening Visualization: Imagine a warm, healing oil flowing into the painful area, softening the hard edges. Practice for 10 minutes.
The Breath Bridge: When pain spikes, instead of fighting it, count 10 slow breaths. Imagine breathing space around the pain.
homework: Notice 'Guarding' behaviors (limping, bracing) and gently try to move normally if safe.
Set a 'Relaxation Alarm' for midday to check in with your tension levels.

modules.title: Module 4 • Challenging Pain Thoughts: The Mental Game
modules.overview: This module tackles the cognitive side of the Gate Control Theory. Specifically, 'Catastrophizing'—the belief that the pain is unbearable and will never end. We identify 'Automatic Negative Thoughts' (ANTs) about pain. e.g., 'I am damaged,' 'My life is over,' 'I am a burden.' We use the 'Thought Record' to challenge these thoughts. Examining the evidence: 'Is it true my life is over? Or is it just different?' We address 'Labeling.' How words like 'agony,' 'stabbing,' and 'killing me' can actually intensify the neural signal. The concept of 'Self-Efficacy' is built. Shifting from 'I can't do anything because of pain' to 'I can do some things despite pain.' We explore identity beyond pain. You are a person *with* pain, not a 'pain patient.' Finally, we create 'Coping Statements.' Powerful, believable mantras to use during flare-ups.
takeaways: Catastrophizing is one of the strongest predictors of pain intensity; changing it reduces pain.
Your language shapes your experience; using neutral words can lower the threat level.
You can feel helpless and be capable at the same time.
You are more than your MRI scan.
exercises: Catastrophe Catching: Catch yourself thinking 'This is terrible' or 'It never ends.' Stop. Take a breath. Replace it with: 'This is a flare-up. I have handled them before. It will pass.'
The Language Swap: Write down 3 intense words you use for pain (e.g., stabbing, burning). Swap them for neutral descriptors (e.g., sharp, warm, intense). Use these for a week.
Evidence Log: Write down 3 things you accomplished this week despite the pain. Prove to your brain that you are capable.
homework: Complete a Thought Record for a moment of high pain distress.
Use your Coping Statements (e.g., 'I am safe,' 'This is temporary') during difficult moments.
Read a book or watch a movie that has nothing to do with health—give your brain a break from the topic.

modules.title: Module 5 • Movement & Meaning: Living Your Values
modules.overview: The final module integrates everything into a life of purpose. We move from 'managing pain' to 'engaging in life.' We use 'Values Clarification.' Identifying what matters to you (family, nature, creativity) independent of your physical ability. We set 'SMART Goals' that are values-based. e.g., 'I want to walk in the park (Goal) to connect with nature (Value).' We create a 'Flare-Up Plan.' A toolkit for bad days so you don't panic or despair. We discuss 'Communication.' How to talk to doctors, family, and employers about your needs without apologizing for your existence. The concept of 'Neuroplasticity' is revisited as a source of long-term hope. Your nervous system can change. Finally, we focus on 'Joy.' Actively scheduling pleasurable activities, because positive emotions are natural painkillers.
takeaways: Pain takes up less space when your life is bigger.
Values give you a 'why' to endure the 'how' of pacing and practice.
A flare-up plan prevents a lapse from becoming a relapse.
You are the expert on your own body.
exercises: Values Compass: Identify your top 3 values. Brainstorm one small activity for each that you can do even on a bad pain day.
The Flare-Up Box: Physically create a box with comforts—heat packs, favorite photos, a list of coping statements, a funny book.
Goal Setting: Set a 3-month goal using the pacing principles. (e.g., 'To walk a 5k by increasing 1 minute per week').
homework: Execute one values-based activity this week.
Write a letter of appreciation to your body for what it *can* do, despite the pain.

aiSupport.systemPrompt: Help the user apply one concrete module step at a time. Do not diagnose. Escalate urgent safety concerns to emergency care.
